We spent 14,000 dollars on AWS before finding the single SQL query causing it.

It happened on a random Tuesday when our database CPU hit 99 percent. Our SaaS was crawling, and customers from our biggest enterprise account in Chicago started pinging us.

Our instinct was to throw money at the problem by upgrading our RDS database. That would have cost an extra 2,000 dollars every month.

Instead, we ran a quick EXPLAIN ANALYZE on our main workspace query. We found a missing index on a foreign key column that had been overlooked during our last major release. Adding that single index took 4 seconds.

The database CPU dropped to 4 percent immediately, and our next bill was back to normal. We learned that scaling is rarely about paying for bigger servers. It is usually about fixing the lazy code we wrote when we were trying to launch fast.

How do you handle cost tracking inside your engineering team without slowing down your shipping speed?

#softwareengineering #bootstrapping #saas

We deleted our favorite product feature after 6 months of absolute silence.

My co-founder and I spent nearly 180 hours building an advanced analytics dashboard. We imagined our users logging in every morning, sipping coffee, and staring at our beautiful custom charts.

The reality was brutal. Only three people clicked the tab over a 90-day period, and two of them did it entirely by accident.

So we killed it. We removed the code, cleaned up the interface, and redirected our energy to improving our CSV export tool, which was actually getting heavy daily use.

Killing features you love hurts your ego. But keeping dead code in your product creates a slow, painful tax on future development. It is better to have a simple tool that solves one real problem than a complex dashboard that nobody looks at.

What is a feature you spent weeks building only to realize your users did not actually want it?

We walked away from a 1.2 million dollar seed term sheet in 2022.

The investor was reputable, and the money would have given us a comfortable two-year runway. It felt like the ultimate validation for our early-stage developer tool.

But during the final partner meeting, we realized their expectations did not align with our vision. They wanted a hyper-growth venture path that required hiring 15 people in six months. We wanted to stay small, profitable, and hyper-focused on our product.

We said no. It was terrifying to sign the rejection email and hit send.

Instead of hiring a massive team, we focused on improving our self-serve onboarding. Today, our team of four generates over 80,000 dollars in monthly recurring revenue without any institutional backing.

If you had to choose between venture capital or complete control over your roadmap, which would you pick and why?

Our best engineering hire had a blank resume and zero big-tech names.

When we posted our open role for a senior backend developer, we received over 400 applications. Most had impressive resumes listing companies like Google, Meta, or Stripe.

But one application stood out. It was a simple link to a GitHub repository where the candidate had built a custom file-sharing tool using Rust and WebRTC.

There was no fancy university name or prestigious corporate background. The readme file explained exactly why they made specific architectural choices, including how they handled packet loss.

We skipped the generic whiteboard coding test. We spent an hour talking about their hobby project instead.

Two weeks later, they joined our team. Within their first month, they optimized our media processing pipeline and saved us 30 percent on our monthly hosting bills.

How do you filter for genuine technical curiosity when hiring for your technical roles?

We replaced our bloated Jira board with a single text document last month.

Our team of eight was spending more time managing tickets, story points, and sub-tasks than writing actual code. Every Monday morning felt like an administrative chore.

We decided to run an experiment. We archived our complex sprint boards and created a simple text document in Notion.

Now, we list three big priorities for the week. Under each priority, we list the raw tasks and assign a name to each.

There are no points, no automated workflows, and no status columns. If a task is done, we put a checkmark next to it. If it is blocked, we talk about it directly on Slack.

This simple change freed up at least three hours of planning meetings every single week. Our shipping velocity actually increased because the team spent less time updating software and more time solving user problems.

How does your team keep project management lightweight without losing track of important tasks?

#productivity #projectmanagement #softwaredevelopment

I spent three hours onboarding our first fifty users manually over Zoom.

When we launched our API tool, we did not have an automated sign-up flow. We did not even have a payment gateway integrated.

Instead, I sent personal emails to every single person who entered their email address on our landing page. I offered to set up their workspace for them during a short video call.

Those calls were exhausting, but they became our secret weapon. I watched exactly where users got confused, where they hesitated, and what questions they asked.

I learned that our documentation was too complex for non-technical users. We rewrote the quick-start guide the next day based on those direct observations.

Doing unscalable things early on is painful. But it gives you a deep understanding of your users that no analytics dashboard or heat map can ever replicate.

What did you learn from your most recent direct interaction with an unhappy customer?

#startups #customersuccess #productgrowth

Building for your imaginary future customers is a fast way to go broke.

A year ago, we started writing code for features we thought a Fortune 500 company would need. We designed multi-tenant permissions, complex audit logs, and custom enterprise reporting.

The problem was that our actual paying customers were small design agencies of three to five people. They did not care about enterprise-grade audit logs. They just wanted our core editor to load faster.

We wasted two months of engineering time building a sports car for customers who only needed a reliable bicycle.

Now, we have a strict rule. We do not write a single line of enterprise code unless a company puts down a deposit first. We focus entirely on the urgent problems of the users who are paying us today.

How do you decide which feature requests to prioritize when your users have wildly different needs?

#softwaredevelopment #productstrategy #saas

We spent 4,200 dollars on paid ads and got exactly zero signups.

We thought we knew how to run targeted campaigns. We set up neat ad groups, designed sleek graphics, and targeted specific keywords on Google and LinkedIn.

The clicks came, but our landing page conversion rate stayed flat at zero percent. It was a painful waste of capital for an early-stage startup.

Frustrated, I decided to write a raw, honest post on a small subreddit for developers. I explained the specific technical challenge we were trying to solve with our tool and asked for feedback.

That single post cost zero dollars to publish. It generated over eighty signups in twenty-four hours and led to our first three paying customers.

Paid acquisition can work, but it rarely works before you have a clear message that resonates with a specific community. Genuine conversations are much harder to scale, but they actually work.

Where did your very first paying customer come from, and how did they find you?

We spent six weeks rewriting our Node backend in Go and regretted it.

Our original API was written in JavaScript. As our user base grew, we started experiencing latency spikes during peak hours.

We fell into the classic developer trap. We assumed JavaScript was the problem and decided a complete rewrite in Go would solve everything.

The rewrite took six weeks of intense work. We had to pause all new feature development and push our product roadmap back.

When we finally deployed the new Go backend, the latency spikes remained. The bottleneck was not the language at all. It was an unoptimized database query that was executing inside a loop.

We could have fixed that query in two hours of debugging. Instead, we wasted a month and a half on a rewrite that we did not need.

What was the most expensive technical mistake you made because you jumped to conclusions too quickly?

I uninstalled Slack from my phone last quarter to save my focus.

As a startup founder, I felt a constant pressure to be available twenty-four hours a day. Every ping from a team member or customer triggered a tiny hit of adrenaline.

I found myself checking channels during dinner, in between meetings, and right before falling asleep. My focus was completely fragmented.

I decided to delete the mobile app entirely. Now, I only check Slack from my laptop during my designated work hours.

My team still has my phone number for real emergencies, but they have only used it once in three months. The company did not collapse, decisions were not delayed, and my productivity actually improved.

Giving yourself space to think deeply is far more valuable than responding to every message in thirty seconds.

How do you set boundaries with your team to protect your deep work time?
